originalGroup.material:
A. Learning to juggle and sharing books

Learning to juggle is easier when dropping a ball is treated as part of the practice. Three balls in the air may be the final aim, but beginning with all three can make it difficult to understand what went wrong.

Start with one soft ball. Throw it gently from one hand to the other, keeping the height fairly consistent. ____1____ A regular path gives the receiving hand a predictable place to wait.

Next, practise with two balls. Follow a simple demonstration and notice when the second throw begins. ____2____ If you hold the second ball until the first has already landed, you lose the rhythm you are trying to establish.

Keep your eyes around the top of the throws rather than chasing each hand. At first, this may feel less secure. ____3____ That wider view helps you notice the pattern instead of making every catch a separate emergency.

Practise in short sessions with room around you. When a ball falls, stop and pick it up rather than trying to run after it among nearby furniture. ____4____ Tired hands and growing frustration rarely make the next attempt easier.

When you introduce the third ball, expect the pattern to break several times. Return to two if necessary. ____5____ What matters is building a movement you understand, not proving that you can avoid every beginner's mistake.

B. Learning to juggle and sharing books

A small box of books appeared beside our community hall last spring. It ____1____ (build) by a retired carpenter, who wanted neighbours to exchange things they had enjoyed reading. A simple sign invited people to take a book or leave one for someone else.

At first, I wondered ____2____ the books would stay dry. The carpenter showed me the roof and the door, explaining how they kept out ordinary rain. After a severe storm, however, someone still needed to check inside.

My sister volunteered ____3____ (visit) the box on her way home from school. She did not have to arrange the books by size or colour. Her job was to notice any wet pages and tell the organiser ____4____ problems that needed attention.

One afternoon, she found a handwritten note inside a novel. It thanked the person ____5____ had left it there, saying that the story had made a long hospital wait more bearable. My sister read the note ____6____ (quiet), then put it back for the next reader.

Since then, several neighbours ____7____ (offer) to help care for the box. Their names are kept on a list so that nobody feels responsible for every day. Sharing books has become ____8____ way of sharing a small task as well. The project is ____9____ (simple) than a library, but it still depends on people giving it some of ____10____ (they) time.

originalGroup.material:
A. Choosing a review and changing a costume

Film reviews can help you choose what to watch, but a review is also a particular person's response. Reading it well involves more than checking whether the final judgment is positive. You need to understand the standards behind that judgment.

Look for the qualities the reviewer values. One may focus on careful plotting, another on visual invention. ____1____ Two reviewers can describe the same feature accurately yet disagree about how much it matters.

Separate a plot summary from an evaluation. A summary tells you what happens; an evaluation explains how effectively the film does its work. ____2____ That explanation gives you something to compare with your own preferences.

Notice how much evidence supports an opinion. A reviewer may call a scene moving without saying what made it so. ____3____ A concrete example can make the judgment easier to understand even if you eventually disagree.

Think about the kind of experience you want. A slow pace praised for allowing reflection might be unwelcome when you want a lively comedy. ____4____ Your disagreement may reflect a different purpose rather than a failure by either you or the critic.

Finally, return to a review after seeing the film if you are interested. ____5____ Comparing your response with the review can reveal a detail you missed or help you explain why a praised moment did not work for you.

B. Choosing a review and changing a costume

The costume for our school performance arrived two weeks before opening night. It looked impressive on the hanger, but when I tried ____1____ (walk) across the stage in it, the long coat caught beneath my shoes. Our costume helper asked me to stop before I fell.

She pinned the bottom temporarily, ____2____ (make) it possible to move while she checked the length. I had worried that changing the coat would spoil its appearance. In fact, it was hard to see the change ____3____ the audience's seats.

The helper explained that clothing for performance had to support action as well as create an image. A sleeve ____4____ covered my hands might suit a still photograph but make it difficult to handle a letter during the scene.

We practised that movement several ____5____ (time). After she had adjusted the sleeve, I could take the letter ____6____ (easy) without looking down. Another actor checked how the coat appeared when I turned away from the lights.

By the next rehearsal, the final changes ____7____ (complete). We kept the removed pieces in case they were needed later. I thanked the helper ____8____ noticing a problem I had first blamed on myself. Learning the part meant understanding how words, movement and costume worked together. The coat no longer felt like something I had to fight; it had become ____9____ useful part of the role. I was able ____10____ (concentrate) on the scene again.

A. Arguing a position and fixing a clock

A classroom debate may require you to defend a position you do not personally hold. The exercise can be valuable if its purpose is to understand an argument rather than to perform certainty. Preparing well means taking the assigned view seriously without pretending that all its claims are beyond question.

Begin by stating the position precisely. A broad slogan may conceal several separate proposals. ____1____ Otherwise, you may spend your preparation defending a claim that the actual debate never required.

Look for the strongest support available to that position. Choosing an obviously weak argument makes the exercise easier but less informative. ____2____ You need to understand why a thoughtful person might find the view persuasive.

Identify its difficult points as well. Acknowledging a limitation does not automatically surrender the whole argument. ____3____ This can lead to a more defensible claim than insisting that the proposal works equally well in every case.

During the debate, listen for what the other side is actually saying. A prepared reply may address an objection nobody has made. ____4____ A brief pause to understand the point can produce a better response than an immediate speech from your notes.

Afterwards, distinguish the quality of your performance from any change in your opinion. ____5____ You may still reject the position while understanding its attraction and limits more clearly than before.

B. Arguing a position and fixing a clock

The clock in our school courtyard had stopped long before I joined the repair club. We were not permitted to work on its mechanism ourselves, but a qualified repairer agreed ____1____ (let) us observe. Before opening the case, she explained the precautions that protected both the clock and the people nearby.

What interested me most ____2____ (be) the number of small adjustments involved. I had imagined one broken part that could simply be replaced. Instead, the repairer first examined how several parts moved in relation to one another.

She described the fault ____3____ (careful), distinguishing it from the wear that could be expected in an old mechanism. We were encouraged to ask questions, but she would not make a movement just to satisfy our ____4____ (curious) if it might damage something.

The following week, we watched the clock ____5____ (return) to its normal position. Its face looked much as it had before. The most important change was one that a passing student might not notice until the hands moved.

Our teacher asked for a short account ____6____ what we had learned. Rather than presenting ____7____ (we) as the people who had repaired it, we described the specialist's work and our role as observers. The repairer, ____8____ patience had made our questions possible, checked the wording. Seeing the clock run again was ____9____ pleasure, but understanding the limits of our own contribution was an ____10____ (equal) important lesson.
